short.titel: SNOWBOARDS TO SOFTWARE: THE SHOPIFY ORIGIN
short.text:
Over five million customers now run on software made for snowboards. Shopify's start was far stranger.

In 2004, friends launched Snowdevil to sell snowboarding gear online. Programmer Lütke was dissatisfied.

So what did he do? He built his own, for Snowdevil's online store.

He used open source Ruby on Rails. The store launched after two months.

In June 2006, the founders launched the platform as Shopify, with Liquid templates.

By 2024, Shopify, born at a snowboard store, processed US$292.3 billion in transactions.

lang.thema: Rockstar North: from an office above a Dundee chip shop to Grand Theft Auto
lang.titel: Rockstar North – CHIP SHOP TO GTA: DMA DESIGN'S WILD RIDE
lang.text:
Grand Theft Auto was once sold for survival money. The studio was DMA Design, now Rockstar North, the maker of Grand Theft Auto. But the strangest part was what its founder sold to survive.

This video answers one question. How did a tiny Dundee studio above a chip shop end up making Grand Theft Auto, and what did it give up along the way?

David Jones grew up in Dundee, where a Timex factory built the ZX Spectrum for Sinclair. At a local computer club, he met Steve Hammond, Russell Kay and a 14-year-old, Mike Dailly. They wanted to make original games, not copy existing ones.

When Timex cut jobs, Jones took £3,000 in voluntary redundancy. He spent it on an Amiga 1000.

A publisher offered a deal. But he feared his game would just become the Amiga version of Zynaps. So he walked away.

He chose Psygnosis instead, with a six-game deal. His game Menace came out in October 1988 after 18 months of work. Jones earned just £0.75 per copy, a deal he later called terrible.

Still, 20,000 sales bought him a car. The sequel, Blood Money, sold 40,000 copies. So he dropped out of university, against his professors' advice.

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

His father-in-law owned a Dundee fish and chip shop called The Deep Sea. He lent Jones small office space above its former location. It opened on 1 August 1989. But the game that made them rich began as a lunch-break joke.

Dailly challenged himself to draw characters recognisable at half the height of another team's. During one lunch break, he animated tiny figures walking in a line and being killed comically. The whole office laughed.

Kay said a game could be built from it. Jones imagined the player stopping the characters from dying. Lemmings arrived in February 1991 and sold 55,000 copies on its first day.

Lemmings sold 20 million copies across 21 platforms. At 25, Jones became a millionaire and bought several luxury cars.

But success had a trap. Psygnosis wanted expansions and sequels, and the studio grew tired of Lemmings. The original deal ended with All New World of Lemmings in 1994.

So Jones looked for new partners. At a trade show, he caught Nintendo's attention with a full-motion video Star Wars clip on the Super Nintendo, something previously believed impossible.

Nintendo signed DMA Design to a two-game contract worth several million pounds. The studio spent around £250,000 fitting its rooms with high-end devices.

Then came Pixar. After Unirally's release, Pixar sued Nintendo over its unicycle characters. The judge ruled for Pixar. Even so, the game sold 300,000 copies.

Meanwhile, Dailly tested how to render 3D buildings from above. His demo let the player control a dinosaur and destroy a city. A colleague then suggested driving the cars instead.

That became Race'n'Chase. In March 1995, BMG Interactive signed a £3.4 million contract for four games. Jones had not told his marketing firm about the deal. That silence would be tested in court.

The money fuelled a hiring spree. Headcount was meant to grow from 40 to 130. The studio built a £500,000 motion capture studio that found little usage.

Then the projects stalled. Body Harvest missed its Nintendo 64 launch. Nintendo cancelled Kid Kirby. And BMG's American division kept pushing to cancel Race'n'Chase because the team missed milestones.

Here was the decision. Jones kept agreeing to projects just to collect sign-on bonuses, with no plans to complete them. At one point, seven or eight projects ran at once.

He also sold the rights to Grand Theft Auto to BMG Interactive, to help keep the studio afloat.

In November 1996, the studio opened a satellite office in Boulder, Colorado. But financial trouble kept growing. Nintendo cancelled Body Harvest after conflicting demands from its Japanese and American branches.

In April 1997, Gremlin Interactive bought DMA Design for £4.2 million. Jones received a 5% stake. Gremlin expected profit within two years, and it made the studio finish games fast, rather than only when good.

Two months later, Gremlin listed on the London Stock Exchange. Jones's stake was valued at £55 million.

But the marketing firm sued for £1.5 million over breach of contract. A Scottish judge called the studio's exclusion of the firm a rather cynical action, and found it was a breach.

The takeover also spun the Boulder studio off. Hammond left to write a Hired Guns remake there. He said he regretted it ever since. The remake was never released.

Then Grand Theft Auto arrived in November 1997. A publicist wanted to market it with controversy. A peer warned of it in the House of Lords, and tabloids called for a ban.

Reviews were mixed. Yet the game quickly sold 500,000 units and generated £25 million.

Bertelsmann then wound down BMG Interactive. Take-Two bought it in March 1998 for US$14.2 million, gaining Grand Theft Auto's intellectual property. Sam Houser moved to Take-Two, and Rockstar Games formed that December.

Gremlin, meanwhile, sank. Poor Body Harvest sales contributed to dire finances, and Infogrames took it over for £24 million. Infogrames focused on child-friendly games and didn't want Grand Theft Auto assets.

So in September 1999, Take-Two bought DMA Design for just £1. It also took on US$12.3 million in debt. Gremlin had paid £4.2 million for it two years earlier.

Grand Theft Auto 2 arrived in October 1999. It sold more than 1 million copies, the first Take-Two game to do so. Then a new satellite studio opened in Leith, Edinburgh.

Jones left in early 2000, unhappy with the overseas ownership. Take-Two closed the Dundee studio that March. Many of its 35 staffers moved to Edinburgh, and the rest were laid off.

In Edinburgh, a core team of 20 built Grand Theft Auto III, inside a total team of 60. It added fully 3D graphics and a third-person view to an open world.

It sold 6 million copies in one year and more than 15 million in total. In March 2002, DMA Design was renamed Rockstar Studios. By May, it was Rockstar North.

Not every idea worked. After Vice City, the studio began Z, a zombie game on a Scottish island. It was in production about a month before the concept lost traction.

San Andreas arrived in October 2004 on a budget under $10 million. In four days, it generated $101 million and sold 2.1 million copies.

Grand Theft Auto IV followed in April 2008. It broke the record for a game's one-day revenue, with $310 million from 3.6 million copies sold.

So how did a chip shop office reach Grand Theft Auto? Not through one clean plan. Jones sold the rights to survive, then sold the studio, and later it went for £1.

But the team and the open-world idea survived under Take-Two. Today Rockstar North is credited with Grand Theft Auto V, the second-best-selling game and most profitable entertainment product of all time.
